name: Kang-Petrov Arms KPR-91B 'Bloc'
description:
The KPR-91B is Kang-Petrov's bullpup variant in 7.62mm Soviet Pattern, and it represents the most significant departure from the KPR family's design philosophy since the caseless experiment. Moving the action behind the trigger group reduces the overall length to 620mm with a full 490mm barrel — the rifle achieves carbine dimensions while retaining full-length ballistics, which is the entire point of the bullpup configuration and the reason Kang-Petrov's engineering team spent three years arguing about whether it was worth the tooling investment. The magazine inserts behind the pistol grip into a receiver that has been structurally redesigned from the stamped-steel heritage into a reinforced polymer shell over a steel chassis — a compromise that the purists hate and the operators who carry it through tight urban corridors appreciate. The trigger pull is longer and heavier than the standard KPR owing to the mechanical linkage required by the bullpup layout, which is the bullpup's original sin and the KPR-91B's primary criticism. Kang-Petrov's solution is to make the trigger as consistent as possible rather than as light as possible — the break is predictable if not pleasant.

The KPR-91B occupies a specific niche in GLMZ's Tier 2 market: operators who work in environments where length matters more than trigger feel. Transit corridor security, building-access contractors, anyone who moves through the megacity's dense lower-level infrastructure where a full-length rifle becomes a liability at every doorway. The 7.62mm Soviet Pattern caliber gives them the punch of the KPR-47 in a package that clears doorframes. The price is higher than the KPR-47 due to the chassis design complexity, which keeps it out of the Tier 1 market and gives it a slightly aspirational quality in the the Gray Zone districts.

The KPR-91B's aesthetics are divisive in GLMZ's rifle culture. The bullpup configuration looks wrong to anyone raised on KPR-47 aesthetics — the magazine behind the grip, the short nose, the absence of visible action forward of the trigger. Operators who grew up with the KPR-47 call it 'backwards' and mean it as criticism. Operators who came to KP rifles through the KPR-91B call the KPR-47 'front-heavy' and mean it as criticism. The two camps have been arguing in GLMZ's underground weapons forums since the KPR-91B's introduction in 2179, and the argument has not resolved. The rifles, meanwhile, do not care.
specifications: caliber: 7.62mm Soviet Pattern effective_range: 420m rate_of_fire: Semi-automatic / Full-automatic magazine_capacity: 30 rounds weight: 3.9 kg
tactical_use: The KPR-91B's tactical identity is built around the combination of 7.62mm Soviet Pattern ballistics in a short-length package. Operators run it in environments where a full-length rifle is a liability — transit corridors, access tunnels, stairwells, the dense micro-architecture of GLMZ's lower-level commercial districts. The longer trigger pull requires adjustment for operators accustomed to the standard KPR trigger, but experienced KPR-91B users report that the consistency of the break compensates for the weight once the muscle memory is built. In close-quarters engagements, the shorter length allows muzzle clearance and target tracking that a full-length KPR-47 cannot match.
cultural_context: The KPR-91B's place in GLMZ rifle culture is that of a contested middle ground. It is too recognizably a KP rifle to be aspirational in the way a Tessera or an Arcturus platform would be, but its departure from the KPR-47's design language marks it as something other than the family inheritance. Operators who carry it are making a choice — they are choosing function over lineage — and in the the Gray Zone districts where lineage matters, that choice is noticed and discussed. The KPR-91B has a stronger following in the mid-tier than the Tier 1 districts for this reason.
known_users: mid-tier fixers working dense urban environments
KP loyalists who work in confined spaces
story_hooks: A KPR-91B with a modified trigger linkage — hand-fitted to achieve a pull weight below Kang-Petrov's minimum specification — was used in a targeted killing inside a Slagworks Industrial transit hub, and the modification suggests a gunsmith with specific knowledge of the 91B's internals; there are only three people in GLMZ with that level of documented expertise, and two of them work for Slagworks.

A the Gray Zone district elder who was one of the first people in GLMZ to carry a KPR-91B when it was introduced in 2179 is being pressured by an Arcturus Civil Security administrator to identify who has been modifying 91Bs in the Pilsen corridor — the elder knows, and the question is whether the pressure is enough to overcome forty years of keeping quiet.
